text: The rain stopped at dawn. Mara opened the shutters and let the gray light in. Somewhere below, a cart wheel groaned over the cobbles.
convention: Three plain declaratives, each closed by a period followed by space or end of text.

text: "Where have you been?" she demanded. He said nothing. "Answer me!"
convention: Three units: a quoted question that ends at the dialogue tag 'demanded.', a declarative, and a final quoted exclamation. Ground truth is three sentences, but the naive regex misses two boundaries: '?' before the closing quote is not followed by whitespace, and the trailing '!' sits before a closing quote at end of text, so the final clause is never closed. Naive returns 2.

text: He shrugged. Then he laughed. Then he was gone.
convention: Three short declaratives separated by period-plus-space.

text: Pi is roughly 3.14, but the engineer rounded it to 3 anyway. Nobody objected.
convention: Decimals (3.14) do not create a sentence because the dot is followed by a digit, not whitespace; only the two real periods count.

text: Wow! Amazing. Truly.
convention: Three terminal units; exclamation and periods each delimit one sentence.

text: Why? Because I said so. That is the end of it.
convention: Question mark and periods each close a sentence; all are followed by space or end.

text: "Run!" he shouted. They scattered into the trees.
convention: Quoted exclamation forms part of the first sentence (the bang is followed by a closing quote, not space, so the unit closes at 'shouted.'); two sentences total, and the naive regex also returns 2.

text: He was born in the U.S.A.
convention: Acronym U.S.A. is a single sentence; the interior dots are followed by letters, only the final dot ends the sentence.

text: She earned her Ph.D.
convention: An abbreviation ending the only sentence; the trailing dot closes one sentence.

text: The room was empty save for a chair, a lamp, and the smell of old paper
convention: No terminal punctuation, but non-empty text counts as one sentence via the fallback.

text: Pi is 3.14159 and e is about 2.718. Both numbers matter to her.
convention: Two decimals do not split; only the two sentence-final periods count.

text: It costs $3.50 today. Buy two before they're gone.
convention: Currency decimal $3.50 is not a boundary; two periods, two sentences.

text:
One sentence here.

Another one here.
convention: Two paragraphs, each a single period-terminated sentence; newlines do not affect the count.

text: The CEO of NASA spoke first. Everyone in the hall fell silent.
convention: All-caps acronyms (NASA, CEO) carry no dots here; two ordinary periods, two sentences.

text: — Are you sure? — Yes, completely.
convention: Dash-led dialogue lines; a question mark and a period each close one sentence.

text: Dr. Reyes arrived late and out of breath. She apologized to the panel.
convention: The title 'Dr.' must not create a sentence; there are two real sentences. The naive regex splits on 'Dr. ' and returns 3.

text: Mr. and Mrs. Dale left without a word. They never came back.
convention: Titles 'Mr.' and 'Mrs.' are abbreviations, not sentence ends; two sentences only. The naive regex splits on both titles and returns 4.

text: Bring bread, milk, eggs, etc. We will need supplies for the week.
convention: 'etc.' should not end a sentence; the true count is two. The naive regex also outputs 2, but for the wrong reason: it ends a sentence at 'etc.' and closes the trailing clause only at end of text, so the right number arrives by coincidence rather than correct segmentation.

text: Some fruits, e.g. apples and plums, are red. I happen to like them.
convention: 'e.g.' is an abbreviation and must not split; only two sentences exist. The naive regex splits after 'e.g.' and returns 3.

text: It was very late, i.e. well past midnight, when she finally called. No one waited up.
convention: 'i.e.' is an abbreviation and does not end a sentence; two sentences total. The naive regex splits after 'i.e.' and returns 3.

text: The meeting is at 9 a.m. sharp, so don't be late.
convention: Time abbreviation 'a.m.' must not split; this is a single sentence. The naive regex splits after 'a.m.' and returns 2.

text: Visit www.example.com for the full schedule. It saves a phone call.
convention: Dots inside a URL must not split. Ground truth is two sentences; the naive regex also returns 2 only because the URL dots are followed by letters, not whitespace — a benign but fragile coincidence.

text: He moved to the U.S.A. last spring. Nobody back home knew.
convention: When the acronym 'U.S.A.' is followed by a space mid-text, its final dot wrongly splits; the true count is two sentences but the naive regex returns 3.

text: "Go home." She turned away without looking back.
convention: A quoted sentence closed by period-then-quote should count; there are two sentences, but the period sits before the closing quote so the naive regex misses the first boundary and returns 1.

text: Stop.Go.Now.
convention: Periods with no following space still terminate sentences; three units, but the naive regex requires whitespace-or-end after the terminal and so collapses them to one.

text: What?! You cannot possibly be serious right now.
convention: An interrobang ('?!') is a single terminal cluster ending one sentence; two sentences total and the naive regex collapses the cluster correctly.

text: No!!! Stop right there and put it down.
convention: Multiple exclamation marks form one terminal cluster; two sentences, which the naive regex collapses correctly.

text: I wondered… then I gathered my coat and left.
convention: A mid-sentence ellipsis (…) marks a trailing-off pause, not a sentence end here; one sentence, but the naive regex treats … as terminal and splits into 2.

text: "I don't know…" she whispered. He only nodded.
convention: The trailing ellipsis belongs to the dialogue clause that ends at 'whispered.'; there are two sentences. The naive regex returns 2 but boundaries are misplaced (it ends a unit at … inside the quote and folds the dialogue tag in), so the count is coincidental.

text: De storm was voorbij. Anna deed de luiken open. Beneden kraakte een kar over de keien.
convention: Drie gewone mededelende zinnen, elk afgesloten met een punt gevolgd door spatie of einde.

text: Dhr. Bakker kwam binnen en hing zijn jas op. Hij zweeg lange tijd.
convention: 'Dhr.' is een aanspreektitel en mag geen zin beëindigen; er zijn twee zinnen. De naïeve regex splitst op 'Dhr. ' en geeft 3.

text: Neem brood, melk, kaas, enz. We hebben genoeg voor de week.
convention: 'enz.' (enzovoort) is een afkorting en sluit geen zin af; het juiste aantal is twee, en de naïeve regex geeft toevallig ook 2 doordat hij de zin bij 'enz.' afkapt en de rest pas op het einde sluit.

text: Veel fruit, bijv. appels en peren, is gezond. Ik hou er erg van.
convention: 'bijv.' (bijvoorbeeld) is een afkorting en mag niet splitsen; er zijn twee zinnen. De naïeve regex splitst op 'bijv. ' en geeft 3.

text: La pluie cessa à l'aube. Mara ouvrit les volets. En bas, une roue grinça sur les pavés.
convention: Trois phrases déclaratives, chacune close par un point suivi d'une espace ou de la fin.

text: M. Dupont est arrivé en retard et essoufflé. Il a souri malgré tout.
convention: 'M.' (Monsieur) est une abréviation et ne termine pas une phrase ; il y a deux phrases. La regex naïve coupe après 'M. ' et renvoie 3.

text: Mme Laurent attendait sous la pluie battante. Elle soupira longuement.
convention: 'Mme' s'écrit sans point en français, donc aucune fausse coupure ; deux phrases, et la regex donne le bon compte.

text: Voir les chiffres détaillés, cf. page 3, avant de conclure. Tout devient clair ensuite.
convention: 'cf.' est une abréviation et ne doit pas couper la phrase ; il y a deux phrases. La regex naïve coupe après 'cf. ' et renvoie 3.

text: Certains fruits, p.ex. les pommes, sont rouges. J'aime beaucoup ça.
convention: 'p.ex.' (par exemple) est une abréviation et ne doit pas créer de phrase ; il y en a deux. La regex naïve coupe après 'p.ex. ' et renvoie 3.

text: Der Sturm war vorüber. Anna öffnete die Läden. Unten knarrte ein Karren über das Kopfsteinpflaster.
convention: Drei einfache Aussagesätze, jeweils mit Punkt und folgendem Leerzeichen oder Textende.

text: Obst, z.B. Äpfel und Birnen, ist gesund. Ich mag es sehr.
convention: 'z.B.' (zum Beispiel) ist eine Abkürzung und beendet keinen Satz; es gibt zwei Sätze. Die naive Regex trennt nach 'z.B. ' und liefert 3.

text: Brot, Milch, Käse usw. Wir brauchen alles für die Woche.
convention: 'usw.' (und so weiter) ist eine Abkürzung und beendet keinen Satz; die richtige Zahl ist zwei, die die naive Regex hier zufällig trifft, weil sie bei 'usw.' trennt und den Rest erst am Ende schließt.

text: Er kam spät, d.h. nach Mitternacht, nach Hause. Niemand hatte gewartet.
convention: 'd.h.' (das heißt) ist eine Abkürzung und darf nicht trennen; es gibt zwei Sätze. Die naive Regex trennt nach 'd.h. ' und liefert 3.

text: La lluvia paró al amanecer. Mara abrió los postigos. Abajo, una rueda chirrió sobre los adoquines.
convention: Tres oraciones declarativas simples, cada una cerrada por un punto seguido de espacio o fin.

text: El Sr. García llegó tarde y sin aliento. Se disculpó ante todos.
convention: 'Sr.' es una abreviatura de tratamiento y no termina una oración; hay dos oraciones. La regex naïve corta tras 'Sr. ' y devuelve 3.

text: La Sra. López esperaba bajo la lluvia. Suspiró con cansancio.
convention: 'Sra.' es una abreviatura y no debe dividir; hay exactamente dos oraciones. La regex naïve corta tras 'Sra. ' y devuelve 3.

text: Trae pan, leche, queso, etc. Necesitamos de todo para la semana.
convention: 'etc.' es una abreviatura y no cierra una oración; el total correcto es dos, y la regex ingenua devuelve 2 por coincidencia al cortar en 'etc.' y cerrar el resto solo al final.

text: Vive en los EE. UU. desde 2010. Le gusta mucho la costa.
convention: 'EE. UU.' (Estados Unidos) es un acrónimo con espacio interno; no debe dividir. Hay dos oraciones, pero la regex cuenta cada punto seguido de espacio y sobreestima a cuatro.
